title: Milk and jasmine at Multan
hookLine: tradition says Multan's holy men sent a brimming cup of milk; Nanak floated a jasmine flower on it
tomorrow: The Guru bows to the disciple

lines: A CUP FILLED TO THE BRIM.
cards: A cup filled to the very brim, carried across a courtyard by someone walking slowly, not daring to breathe. Bhai Gurdas records no words with it. The cup itself is the message.
He tells this at Multan. When Baba Nanak arrived, the pirs of Multan, its holy men, came to him with a cup brimming with milk. And Nanak answered with no words either.

teach.h: THE CUP: THIS CITY IS FULL.
teach.b: Start with the cup. Sikhs read it as the pirs' polite, pointed message: this city is already full of holy men. There's no room for another.
Like milk to the brim, one more drop and it spills. Now the answer.

teach.h: A JASMINE FLOWER ON THE MILK.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas says Baba took a jasmine flower and put it in the milk. That's all. In the telling Sikhs pass on, not a drop spills, and the milk now carries a scent it didn't have before.
The reply does several things at once. It agrees: yes, the cup is full. It doesn't argue that there's room, or push anyone aside.
It doesn't spill the milk, which would have been an insult to the pirs and their city.
And it shows that something light enough, gentle enough, can still be added to a full place without taking anything from it. It also speaks the pirs' own language.
They said it with a cup, and Nanak answered the same way, courteously, and still said what he came to say.

teach.h: LIKE A RIVER INTO THE SEA.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas closes the scene with a picture of his own: it was like the Ganges merging into the ocean.

A great river doesn't make the sea overflow. It comes in, and becomes part of it. Hear that the way Bhai Gurdas tells it, not as a victory over the holy men of Multan, but as a meeting where nothing was lost.

how: Sikhs retell the story of the milk and the jasmine at Multan as a picture of humility: entering a full place gently, adding fragrance without pushing anyone aside.

o: the city where pirs brought Nanak a brimming cup
a fort where the Gurus kept horses and arms
a river where Nanak bathed before dawn each day

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Nanak tipped out some milk to make room
he put a jasmine flower in it, and in the telling, not a drop spilled.
the pirs of Multan came with a cup brimming with milk
Bhai Gurdas says the cup was full, and Nanak answered with a flower.
Bhai Gurdas tells it as a victory over Multan's holy men
his picture is a river merging into the sea: a meeting, nothing lost.

games.q: you've arrived in a city well-known for its holy men. they bring you a cup of milk filled to the brim. what do you do?
o: send it back and insist there's room.
put a jasmine flower in the milk.
drink it and move on to the next town.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas says Baba put a jasmine flower in the milk. in the telling, nothing spilled, and the cup carried a scent it didn't have before.

practice: Bring to mind a crowded place in your life, a busy household, a tense team, a group chat moving too fast, and choose one small, light thing you could add without taking anyone's space: a cup of tea set down beside someone, a short kind message, a flower in a glass on the table.
Picture it floating there, spilling nothing, and if you pray, say Waheguru over that room.

wordCard.voice: Multan, the city whose pirs sent a cup brimful of milk, and received back a jasmine flower floating on it without spilling a drop.

carryVoice: Your line: room for a flower. A full cup, and still something sweet to add. Day seven hundred six, done.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 44 (Multan: the cup of milk and the jasmine)
